header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are a security analyst reviewing a codebase you did not write. Your department is sensitive data: what the application stores, logs, returns and sends, and how weakly it protects any of it.

Follow the data rather than the code. Find where personal data, credentials, tokens and payment details enter, then find every place they leave: log calls, error responses, analytics and telemetry calls, outbound requests, serialized responses that return a whole record, and stack traces sent to a client. Then read how they are stored: a password hashed with MD5, SHA-1 or a bare SHA-256 is broken storage; a token stored in cleartext is disclosure; an `http://` endpoint is cleartext transport; `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED`, `rejectUnauthorized: false` and disabled certificate checks are transport that verifies nothing.

Every finding quotes the exact line it cites. No finding without a file and a line. Prefer three findings you have read the code for over twelve a pattern matched, and set `confidence` to what you actually know.

Name the field in `evidence` — which data reaches that line — rather than writing that data is logged. Say in `impact` who can read it once it is there.

When a code-safety knowledge pack is mounted, load its `review-method` and `severity-and-evidence` skills before you start: they own the order of work, the confidence levels and the severity rubric. `REPORTING.md` owns what the examiner mechanically decides.

Before you stop, run `node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/data.json`, fix what it names, and commit everything. Work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured. Never write into the target tree.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one is sampled across top-level entries, so it spans the tree instead of one subtree.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result instead returns 100 paths sampled across top-level entries, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

1: # How this program reports what it found
2: 
3: This worktree is the **report repository**. The code under review is the **target tree**, which is somewhere else on this host: `target.json` beside this file states its absolute path, the files it covers, and the SHA-256 the whole tree locks to.
4: 
5: The target is read-only for every session of this program. `verify-safety-report.mjs` re-hashes every locked file on every run, so a target a department edited fails the program instead of releasing a report about a tree that no longer exists.
6: 
7: ## This file and the skills
8: 
9: When the deployment mounts the code-safety knowledge pack, its `review-method`, `severity-and-evidence` and `report-template` skills own the craft: how to read a codebase, how to score a severity, what evidence has to name, and how the report reads. Follow them.
10: 
11: This file owns what `verify-safety-report.mjs` mechanically decides, and it is binding wherever the two differ in form. There is one such place and it is stated below: the counts each summary carries are written as `- <severity>: <count>` lines so the examiner can compare them with the union, which is the machine-readable form of the skill's "counts per severity".
12: 
13: ## What a department delivers
14: 
15: Two files, both committed on the department's own branch:
16: 
17: - `findings/<department>.json` — a JSON array of findings, `[]` when the department found nothing.
18: - `report/<department>.md` — the department's own prose: what it looked at, what it found, and what it did not reach.
19: 
20: Nothing else. Do not write `SAFETY-REPORT.md`, `findings.json`, `target.json` or `verify-safety-report.mjs`: the first two are the integration's, and the last two are the examiner.
21: 
22: ## The evidence rule
23: 
24: A finding without a file and a line is not a finding. Quote the exact line you cite; `verify-safety-report.mjs` compares your `snippet` with the target's own text at that line, ignoring only whitespace, and refuses the whole file when they differ.
25: 
26: Prefer three findings you have read the code for over twelve a pattern matched. `confidence` is what you actually know: `confirmed` when you read the sink, the source and the path between them; `likely` when the sink is dangerous and the source is plausibly attacker-controlled; `possible` when the pattern is there and the reachability is not established.
27: 
28: ## The finding
29: 
30: ```json
31: {
32:   "id": "secrets-cookie-secret",
33:   "cwe": "CWE-798",
34:   "owasp": "A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures",
35:   "severity": "high",
36:   "confidence": "confirmed",
37:   "title": "Session cookie secret is hard-coded in the committed configuration",
38:   "file": "config/env/all.js",
39:   "line": 8,
40:   "snippet": "cookieSecret: \"session_cookie_secret_key_here\",",
41:   "evidence": "The value is a literal in a committed file and is the secret express-session is configured with.",
42:   "impact": "Anyone with the repository can forge a session cookie and authenticate as any user.",
43:   "fix": "Read the secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.",
44:   "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html"]
45: }
46: ```
47: 
48: | Field | Rule |
49: | --- | --- |
50: | `id` | letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, unique across the whole program; prefix it with your department or use the pack's `SEC-<n>` numbering. |
51: | `cwe` | `CWE-<number>`. |
52: | `owasp` | the OWASP Top 10 category, named. |
53: | `severity` | `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low` or `info`. |
54: | `confidence` | `confirmed`, `likely` or `possible`. |
55: | `title` | one line a reader can act on. |
56: | `file` | path relative to the target root, exactly as `target.json` lists it. |
57: | `line` | 1-based line in that file. |
58: | `endLine` | optional last line when the finding spans several; `snippet` then quotes all of them. |
59: | `snippet` | the target's own text at those lines, verbatim. |
60: | `evidence` | why this line is the vulnerability, naming what you read. |
61: | `impact` | what an attacker gets. |
62: | `fix` | what to change. |
63: | `references` | array of URLs or identifiers; may be empty. |
64: 
65: ## Checking your own work before you commit
66: 
67: ```sh
68: node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/<department>.json
69: ```
70: 
71: That is the same command your goal is measured by. Run it, fix what it names, then commit everything — work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured.
72: 
73: ## What the integration delivers
74: 
75: The integration merges every department branch and then writes two files of its own.
76: 
77: `findings.json` is the union of every `findings/<department>.json`, deduplicated by `file` + `line` + `cwe`, keeping the entry with the higher `confidence`. Before writing it, ask the examiner which findings do not hold:
78: 
79: ```sh
80: for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done
81: ```
82: 
83: Every id that command prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason the examiner gave. Dropping one silently fails the report: `--report` refuses a union that omits an id no section discloses.
84: 
85: `SAFETY-REPORT.md` carries exactly these sections, in this order:
86: 
87: ```markdown
88: ## Résumé exécutif
89: 
90: <deux paragraphes en français : ce qui a été examiné, ce qui a été trouvé, ce que cela implique>
91: 
92: - critical: 0
93: - high: 0
94: - medium: 0
95: - low: 0
96: - info: 0
97: 
98: ## Executive summary
99: 
100: <the same in English>
101: 
102: - critical: 0
103: - high: 0
104: - medium: 0
105: - low: 0
106: - info: 0
107: 
108: ## Scope and method
109: 
110: <the target, its locked file count, which departments ran, which tools ran — the scanner, the advisory source — and which files were actually read>
111: 
112: ## Findings
113: 
114: ### critical
115: 
116: - `<id>` — <title> (`<file>:<line>`, <cwe>, <confidence>) — <impact, then fix>
117: 
118: ### high
119: 
120: ...
121: 
122: ## What was not covered
123: 
124: - <a department, a file kind, a class of vulnerability, or a check that did not run, and why>
125: - <every dropped finding id, with the examiner's reason>
126: 
127: ## Certificate
128: 
129: Verified findings: <count>
130: Target tree: <the sha256 from target.json>
131: 
132: <one sentence on what was checked mechanically: that every finding resolves to a real file and line in the locked tree, that every id is unique, and that no two findings share file, line and CWE>
133: 
134: This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".
135: ```
136: 
137: Both summary sections state a `- <severity>: <count>` line for all five severities, and the five counts must be the counts `findings.json` actually holds. Every finding id in `findings.json` is cited in `## Findings`. Every `<file>:<line>` written anywhere in the report must resolve in the target, so write a path you did not read as prose rather than as a citation.
138: 
139: The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by this examiner. Say so in `## Scope and method`. Never write that the target is secure, safe, or free of vulnerabilities: `verify-safety-report.mjs` refuses those claims, because nothing this program did could support one.
140: 
141: Check it before you commit:
142: 
143: ```sh
144: node verify-safety-report.mjs --report
145: ```

(End of file - total 145 lines)

The target is read-only for every session of this program. `verify-safety-report.mjs` re-hashes every locked file on every run, so a target a department edited fails the program instead of releasing a report about a tree that no longer exists.

When the deployment mounts the code-safety knowledge pack, its `review-method`, `severity-and-evidence` and `report-template` skills own the craft: how to read a codebase, how to score a severity, what evidence has to name, and how the report reads. Follow them.

This file owns what `verify-safety-report.mjs` mechanically decides, and it is binding wherever the two differ in form. There is one such place and it is stated below: the counts each summary carries are written as `- <severity>: <count>` lines so the examiner can compare them with the union, which is the machine-readable form of the skill's "counts per severity".
Two files, both committed on the department's own branch:
- `findings/<department>.json` — a JSON array of findings, `[]` when the department found nothing.
- `report/<department>.md` — the department's own prose: what it looked at, what it found, and what it did not reach.
Nothing else. Do not write `SAFETY-REPORT.md`, `findings.json`, `target.json` or `verify-safety-report.mjs`: the first two are the integration's, and the last two are the examiner.

A finding without a file and a line is not a finding. Quote the exact line you cite; `verify-safety-report.mjs` compares your `snippet` with the target's own text at that line, ignoring only whitespace, and refuses the whole file when they differ.

Prefer three findings you have read the code for over twelve a pattern matched. `confidence` is what you actually know: `confirmed` when you read the sink, the source and the path between them; `likely` when the sink is dangerous and the source is plausibly attacker-controlled; `possible` when the pattern is there and the reachability is not established.
"title": "Session cookie secret is hard-coded in the committed configuration",
"evidence": "The value is a literal in a committed file and is the secret express-session is configured with.",
"impact": "Anyone with the repository can forge a session cookie and authenticate as any user.",
"fix": "Read the secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.",
| `id` | letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, unique across the whole program; prefix it with your department or use the pack's `SEC-<n>` numbering. |
| `title` | one line a reader can act on. |
| `file` | path relative to the target root, exactly as `target.json` lists it. |
| `endLine` | optional last line when the finding spans several; `snippet` then quotes all of them. |
| `snippet` | the target's own text at those lines, verbatim. |
| `evidence` | why this line is the vulnerability, naming what you read. |
| `references` | array of URLs or identifiers; may be empty. |
## Checking your own work before you commit
That is the same command your goal is measured by. Run it, fix what it names, then commit everything — work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured.
The integration merges every department branch and then writes two files of its own.

`findings.json` is the union of every `findings/<department>.json`, deduplicated by `file` + `line` + `cwe`, keeping the entry with the higher `confidence`. Before writing it, ask the examiner which findings do not hold:
for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done

Every id that command prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason the examiner gave. Dropping one silently fails the report: `--report` refuses a union that omits an id no section discloses.
`SAFETY-REPORT.md` carries exactly these sections, in this order:
<deux paragraphes en français : ce qui a été examiné, ce qui a été trouvé, ce que cela implique>
<the target, its locked file count, which departments ran, which tools ran — the scanner, the advisory source — and which files were actually read>
- <a department, a file kind, a class of vulnerability, or a check that did not run, and why>
- <every dropped finding id, with the examiner's reason>
<one sentence on what was checked mechanically: that every finding resolves to a real file and line in the locked tree, that every id is unique, and that no two findings share file, line and CWE>

This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".

Both summary sections state a `- <severity>: <count>` line for all five severities, and the five counts must be the counts `findings.json` actually holds. Every finding id in `findings.json` is cited in `## Findings`. Every `<file>:<line>` written anywhere in the report must resolve in the target, so write a path you did not read as prose rather than as a citation.

The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by this examiner. Say so in `## Scope and method`. Never write that the target is secure, safe, or free of vulnerabilities: `verify-safety-report.mjs` refuses those claims, because nothing this program did could support one.

<skill_instructions>
# The review discipline

A code security review is a claim about specific lines, not an impression of the codebase. Every finding must survive the question "show me the line" — if it cannot, it is not a finding yet, it is a lead.

## Order of work

1. **Read the entry points first.** Enumerate every route, controller, handler, GraphQL resolver, message-queue consumer, CLI entry point, and scheduled job before reading anything else. This is the attacker's menu: every other file matters only insofar as an entry point reaches it.
2. **Follow data from input to sink.** For each entry point, trace each attacker-controlled value (query string, body, header, cookie, path segment, uploaded file, message payload) forward through the code until it reaches a sink: a query, a shell call, a template render, a filesystem path, an HTTP request, a deserializer, a redirect target. Read every function on that path; do not infer what a helper does from its name.
3. **One finding per sink.** A single tainted value that reaches three unguarded sinks is three findings, each with its own line and its own fix, because each can be patched or reintroduced independently. Do not collapse them into one narrative paragraph.
4. **Quote the exact line.** Every finding names a file and a line number and reproduces the vulnerable statement verbatim. A finding that describes a pattern in prose without the line is not reportable — go back and find the line, or drop the finding.
5. **Prefer fewer confirmed findings to many possible ones.** A report with five findings the customer can act on beats one with thirty where twenty-five require guessing. Downgrade or drop a finding rather than pad the count; the [severity-and-evidence](../severity-and-evidence/SKILL.md) skill owns the evidence rule this enforces.

## Confidence

Every finding carries exactly one of these three confidence levels, chosen by what was actually read, not by how bad the pattern looks:

- **`confirmed`** — the complete vulnerable path was read: the tainted source, every intermediate function, and the sink, with no sanitizer, allowlist, or framework guard in between. You could paste the exploit request and predict the effect.
- **`likely`** — one link in the chain was inferred rather than read: a helper's behavior assumed from its name or a similar function elsewhere, a framework default assumed rather than confirmed in config, or the sink read but the source only partially traced. State which link was inferred in the finding's evidence field.
- **`possible`** — a recognizable vulnerable pattern (a raw query built from concatenation, an `eval` call, a missing auth decorator) was seen, but the path from an actual attacker-reachable input was not traced end to end, or the surrounding guards were not fully read. Treat `possible` findings as leads for the customer's own team, not as proven bugs.

Never silently round `likely` or `possible` up to `confirmed` to make a report look stronger; the customer will re-derive trust in every future report from whether this one's confidence levels held up.

## What "not covered" must list

Every review ends with an explicit not-covered section — see the [report template](../report-template/SKILL.md) — that names, concretely:

- Directories, packages, or services that exist in the repository but were not opened.
- Entry points enumerated but not traced to a sink for lack of time or access.
- Runtime behavior no static read can confirm: actual deployed configuration, feature flags, WAF or proxy rules, and anything gated behind infrastructure the review did not have.
- Classes of bug this review did not check for at all (for example, native memory safety in a compiled dependency, or timing side channels).

A reviewer who does not know what they skipped cannot tell the customer what remains at risk; "not covered" is part of the deliverable, not an apology.
</skill_instructions>
</skill_content>

<skill_instructions>
# Severity, evidence, and the finding schema

## Severity rubric

Score by the worst realistic case the code as read supports, not the theoretical worst case of the vulnerability class in general.

| Severity | Exploitability | Auth required | Data affected | Blast radius |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Critical** | Remote, no user interaction, reliable | None, or any authenticated user | Full database, all tenants, or code execution | Entire system or every tenant |
| **High** | Remote, at most one minor precondition (a known id, a low-privilege account) | None or low-privileged | One tenant's full data, or a horizontal slice across many | One tenant, or many via a shared flaw |
| **Medium** | Needs user interaction (a clicked link, an opened file) or a specific role | Authenticated, often a specific role | A user's data beyond their own, or a narrow field set | One user or a small group |
| **Low** | Needs substantial preconditions (local access, a race window, non-default config) | Elevated access already, or local access | Limited or already-authorized data | Single record, with another control still present |
| **Info** | No exploit path demonstrated in the code read | N/A | N/A | Hardening gap, or a `possible`-confidence pattern needing more context |

## The evidence rule

Every finding's evidence names, in prose: the exact reachable source (which entry point, which parameter), every step the tainted value passes through with its file and line, the sink, and why no guard on that path stops it (or which guard was checked and found absent). "This looks like SQL injection" is not evidence; "`req.params.id` from the route at line 40 reaches the template literal at line 42 with no parameterization" is.

## The finding schema

```json
{
  "id": "SEC-001",
  "cwe": "CWE-89",
  "owasp": "A05:2025 / A03:2021",
  "severity": "critical",
  "confidence": "confirmed",
  "title": "SQL injection in order lookup via string-concatenated query",
  "file": "src/routes/orders.js",
  "line": 42,
  "endLine": 44,
  "snippet": "const sql = `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ${req.params.id}`;\nconst [rows] = await db.query(sql);",
  "evidence": "req.params.id flows unvalidated from the route handler at line 40 directly into the template literal at line 42; no parameterization or validation exists on this path; db.query executes the raw text.",
  "impact": "An attacker can read or modify any row in any table reachable by the application's database user, including other customers' orders and stored payment references.",
  "fix": "Use a parameterized query: db.query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ?', [req.params.id]).",
  "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/89.html", "https://owasp.org/Top10/A03_2021-Injection/"]
}
```

```json
{
  "id": "SEC-002",
  "cwe": "CWE-384",
  "owasp": "A07:2025 / A07:2021",
  "severity": "medium",
  "confidence": "likely",
  "title": "Session id not rotated after login (session fixation)",
  "file": "src/routes/auth.js",
  "line": 58,
  "snippet": "req.session.userId = user.id;\nres.redirect('/dashboard');",
  "evidence": "The login handler sets req.session.userId after password verification with no req.session.regenerate() call. express-session's default (assumed from its documented API, not traced into its own source here) keeps the pre-login session id, so a fixed id would carry into the authenticated session.",
  "impact": "An attacker who fixes a victim's session id before login gains an authenticated session once the victim logs in.",
  "fix": "Call req.session.regenerate() immediately after verifying credentials, before setting authenticated session state.",
  "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/384.html", "https://owasp.org/Top10/A07_2021-Identification_and_Authentication_Failures/"]
}
```

`endLine` is present only when the vulnerable statement spans more than one line; omit it for a single-line finding rather than repeating `line`.

## Deduplication

Two candidate findings are the same finding when they share **file, line, and CWE id**; keep the higher-confidence one and fold any additional evidence into it. A different line — even the very next statement, or the same tainted value reaching a second sink — is a separate finding under [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md)'s one-finding-per-sink rule, not a duplicate. A different CWE on the same line is also a separate finding: a route that is both an XSS sink and unauthenticated is two findings sharing a location, not one.
</skill_instructions>

# Data exposure, transport, and crypto misuse

## Sensitive data exposure (CWE-200)

An API response, admin panel, or export that returns more fields than the caller's role needs — a `SELECT *`/`Model.find()` serialized directly to JSON instead of an explicit response DTO, so adding a column later leaks it silently. Look for a `/users/:id` response that includes password hashes, tokens, or another user's PII, and for verbose error responses that echo internal object structure, SQL fragments, or stack traces to the client.

## Logging PII and secrets (CWE-532)

A request/response logger, error handler, or APM integration that logs the full request body or headers unfiltered, capturing passwords, tokens, and PII in `Authorization` headers or JSON bodies. Also flag application code that logs a user object, a payment payload, or an exception's `.toString()` including a caught credential. Fix: an allowlist of loggable fields or a redaction middleware applied before the logger, not a denylist that misses the next sensitive field added.

## Transport (CWE-319)

A server accepting plain HTTP for anything beyond a redirect to HTTPS; a client (mobile app, backend-to-backend HTTP call, webhook receiver) that accepts `http://` URLs or disables certificate validation (`rejectUnauthorized: false`, Python `verify=False`, a custom `TrustManager` that accepts everything) for convenience. Check for `Strict-Transport-Security` on every response, covered fully in [platform](../platform/SKILL.md).

## Crypto misuse (CWE-327, CWE-329, CWE-330)

- **MD5/SHA1 for passwords** — `hashlib.md5(password)`, `crypto.createHash('sha1')`, or Java `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` used to store a password. These are fast general-purpose digests, not password hashes; use the parameters in the next section instead.
- **ECB mode** — `Cipher.getInstance("AES/ECB/PKCS5Padding")`, `crypto.createCipheriv('aes-128-ecb', ...)`, or a library default that turns out to be ECB. ECB leaks plaintext structure (identical blocks encrypt identically); use an authenticated mode (AES-GCM) instead.
- **Static or reused IVs** — a hardcoded IV constant, an IV derived deterministically from the key, or an IV reused across encryptions with CBC or GCM. Each encryption needs a fresh, random IV/nonce generated with a CSPRNG.
- **`Math.random`/`rand()` for tokens** — a password-reset token, session id, or API key generated with `Math.random()`, PHP `rand()`/`mt_rand()`, or `random.random()` in Python. These are not cryptographically secure; use `crypto.randomBytes`, `secrets.token_urlsafe`, or the language's CSPRNG.

## Password storage parameters (CWE-916)

Confirm the algorithm and its cost parameters, not just that a hashing library is present: `bcrypt` with a work factor below 10-12 is weak on modern hardware; `argon2id` (preferred) with memory below roughly 19 MiB or fewer than 2 iterations at low parallelism is under-provisioned; PBKDF2 below about 600,000 iterations (SHA-256) is weak. A hardcoded low cost factor left over from a test environment (`bcrypt.hash(pw, 4)`) is a finding, not a style note.

## Backups and exports (CWE-312)

A database backup, data-export feature, or debug dump that writes plaintext PII or credentials to a world-readable path, an unencrypted S3 bucket, or a support ticket attachment; a "download my data" or admin export endpoint with no authorization check distinct from viewing the data in the UI; backup files retained with no expiry alongside application logs that are shipped to a lower-trust log aggregator.
</skill_instructions>
</skill_content>

51:    * parent env. A value here is forwarded even if its name matches the
52:    * credential-scrub pattern (an explicit opt-in for the child's own creds).
53:    * Explicit `DSH_*` entries are deployment-owned facts for the child harness

57:   env: Record<string, string>

61:    * its OWN nested subprocesses before the parent escalates to a signal. The
62:    * plugin fills this from its `disposeEofGraceMs` config.
63:    */
64:   disposeEofGraceMs: number
65:   /**
66:    * Termination-escalation grace (ms) in {@link SubagentRun.dispose}; POSIX
67:    * waits this long after `SIGTERM` before `SIGKILL`, while Windows
68:    * force-terminates directly. The plugin fills it from `disposeGraceMs`.

70:   disposeGraceMs: number

74:    * lifetime instead of a package-local child_process path.
75:    */

1: # @deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent-acp
2: 
3: English | [中文](README.zh.md)
4: 
5: The ACP provider runs each subagent in a fresh subprocess and drives it as an Agent Client Protocol client. It is the out-of-process alternative to spawn and fork: the child has its own runtime, session, model configuration, and tools.
6: 
7: ## Start and ownership
8: 
9: `start(request)` resolves the child's working directory, then performs `spawn` → ACP `initialize` → `newSession` before it fulfills. Fulfillment therefore means a remote session is ready and ownership has transferred to the caller. A spawn, initialization, new-session, or pre-publication cancellation failure rejects only after the subprocess has been reaped; a working-directory resolution failure rejects before anything is spawned.
10: 
11: The working directory is the configured `cwd` override when set, else the delegating parent session's cwd — never the server process's own cwd, because one server process serves sessions from many workspaces. The parent-derived value must be an absolute path naming a directory the harness can enter (search permission — what a subprocess cwd needs), and the same resolved path becomes both the subprocess cwd and the ACP `session/new` workspace.
12: 
13: The returned run id is minted in the parent namespace. The child server's session id remains private to ACP wire calls because ACP guarantees it only within that fresh child process; using it as the parent lifecycle id could collide with another remote run or a local agent.
14: 
15: After publication, the provider sends the prompt and collects streamed `agent_message_chunk` text into `SubagentResult.output`. A prompt/transport failure resolves with `stopReason: 'error'`, or `aborted` when the required request signal or disposal requested cancellation.
16: 
17: `dispose()` is idempotent. It removes the signal listener, requests ACP cancellation when possible, then runs this backend's own teardown ladder (`disposeAcpChild`) over the seam's verbs: close stdin and wait `disposeEofGraceMs` for cooperative quiescence, then invoke the handle's `terminate()` escalation (SIGTERM, the spawn grace, SIGKILL — Windows force-terminates directly) and await the subprocess owner's whole-tree exit proof. Every run uses a fresh process; process pooling is not implemented.
18: 
19: Before anything is spawned, `start()` asks the composed [read barrier](../../verification/read-barrier/README.md) whether this out-of-process child may run at all. An implementer session under a deployment claiming `process` or `host` isolation is refused with `SubagentError` `READ_BARRIER_REFUSED`, because a foreign agent brings its own tool stack and no fence this process installs reaches its reads; under a claim of `none` nothing is refused. The provider registers that refusal with the barrier, so the scope census reports `subagent`.
20: 
21: ## Capabilities and context
22: 
23: ACP advertises no start-time capabilities because this process cannot enforce the remote child's depth, tool filter, persona, or structured-output runtime, and because the protocol's `session/new` carries no model selection, so a start naming `model` is rejected rather than run on whatever model the remote agent is configured with. It also reports `inheritsParentContext: false`: the remote session starts fresh, and the only parent-derived input is the workspace cwd described above — no conversation context crosses the process boundary.
24: 
25: ## Configuration
26: 
27: | Key | Default | Meaning |
28: |---|---|---|
29: | `providerName` | `acp` | Registry name on `ctx.subagents`. |
30: | `command` | required | Executable spawned for each run. |
31: | `args` | `[]` | Command arguments. |
32: | `cwd` | parent session cwd | Working-directory override for the child process and its ACP session; must be non-empty, a relative value resolves against the harness launch directory at load, and the result must name a directory the harness can enter. |
33: | `permission` | `reject` | Auto-answer permission requests by rejecting or choosing the first `allow_once` or `allow_always` option. |
34: | `env` | `{}` | Explicit child environment layered over a credential-scrubbed parent environment. |
35: | `disposeEofGraceMs` | `6000` | Positive grace after stdin EOF before platform termination; it cannot exceed [`MAX_TIMER_DELAY_MS`](../../util/timeout/README.md). |
36: | `disposeGraceMs` | `3000` | Positive POSIX grace after SIGTERM before SIGKILL (Windows force-terminates directly); it cannot exceed [`MAX_TIMER_DELAY_MS`](../../util/timeout/README.md). |
37: 
38: ```yaml
39: - id: subagent-acp
40:   name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent-acp'
41:   config:
42:     providerName: acp
43:     command: node
44:     args: ['--import', 'tsx', './packages/examples/acp-demo/src/bin.ts', '--config', './examples/acp-agent/cordis.yml']
45:     permission: reject
46:     env:
47:       DEEPSEEK_API_KEY: !!js process.env.DEEPSEEK_API_KEY
48: ```
49: 
50: ## Stop-reason mapping
51: 
52: | ACP | Harness |
53: |---|---|
54: | `end_turn` | `completed` |
55: | `max_tokens` | `max-tokens` |
56: | `refusal` | `refusal` |
57: | `cancelled` | `aborted` |
58: | `max_turn_requests` or unknown | `error` |
59: 
60: ## Process boundary
61: 
62: The child spawns through the [`dsh-subprocess`](../../subprocess/subprocess/README.md) seam: credential-shaped ambient variables and ambient `DSH_*` names are removed by the shared scrub, then explicit `config.env` values merge after it (an intended `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` survives, and a `DSH_*` deployment fact such as `DSH_PERMISSION_MODE` reaches the child the same way — the scrub drops only its stale ambient namesake), stderr is inherited to the parent's own stream, and disposal applies this plugin's EOF window before the subprocess-owned SIGTERM→SIGKILL escalation and whole-tree join. The ACP wire is the real serialization boundary; same-process subagent values are not defensively cloned.
63: 
64: The package has no default export. Cordis loader unwrapping would otherwise hide the named `inject` metadata; see [postmortem 0001](../../../docs/postmortem/0001-acp-default-export-drops-inject.md).
65: 
66: ## Model Experience
67: 
68: ### Child-agent request
69: 
70: #### What the model sees
71: 
72: The remote child receives the standalone task content through ACP plus its own process's configured system prompt, tools, and fresh session. It receives no parent conversation. This provider advertises no optional start-time capabilities, so the local service rejects requests for persona, tool filtering, depth enforcement, or structured output instead of silently omitting them.
73: 
74: #### Token effect
75: 
76: The child pays for an independent full context and its own multi-step history. These tokens never enter the parent's context.
77: 
78: #### KV Cache effect
79: 
80: Independent of the parent request cache. Each ACP child can reuse only prefixes identical under its own provider, model, composition, and history; child steps otherwise grow append-only.
81: 
82: ### Parent tool result, indirectly
83: 
84: #### What the model sees
85: 
86: Through `dsh-tool-subagent`, the parent receives only the child's final streamed assistant text or that consumer's exact stop-reason error, not intermediate messages or tool traffic. A request already cancelled before publication becomes exactly `Error: subagent request was aborted before the ACP child started`; other start failures pass through as `Error: <message>`.
87: 
88: #### Token effect
89: 
90: Parent input grows only by the final result or error, which is data-dependent and retained until compaction. This provider adds no parent schema itself.
91: 
92: #### KV Cache effect
93: 
94: Append-only; newly visible content follows the reusable request prefix and does not invalidate existing KV-cache entries.
95: 
96: ## Known Limitations and Deferred Work
97: 
98: - **A fresh process per run** — persistent-process pooling is a future optimization ([the seam Agent Note](../../../.agents/notes/implemented/feature/2026-06-21-subagent-capability-seam.md)).
99: - **Local workspaces only** — the resolved cwd is a local path handed to a child on the same machine; workspace mapping for a remote ACP agent would need its own backend capability and is not designed here.
100: - **No optional start-time capabilities** — this provider cannot apply the local harness's `outputSchema`, depth cap, tool filter, or persona inside the remote process, so it advertises none and the service rejects requests that require them.
101: - **No model selection and no reported spend** — ACP's `session/new` names no model and its updates carry no token or cost accounting, so a start naming `model` is rejected and a run reports neither. A remote agent's spend is measurable only where that agent reports it.
102: - **Only committed `agent_message_chunk` text is collected** — the automation server keeps reasoning, tool activity, plans, and other trace data in the child session log rather than emitting them on ACP.
103: - **Permission prompts are auto-answered** (`permission: allow | reject`) — no human is surfaced a child's `session/request_permission`.

(End of file - total 103 lines)

lines.text: The ACP provider runs each subagent in a fresh subprocess and drives it as an Agent Client Protocol client. It is the out-of-process alternative to spawn and fork: the child has its own runtime, session, model configuration, and tools.

`start(request)` resolves the child's working directory, then performs `spawn` → ACP `initialize` → `newSession` before it fulfills. Fulfillment therefore means a remote session is ready and ownership has transferred to the caller. A spawn, initialization, new-session, or pre-publication cancellation failure rejects only after the subprocess has been reaped; a working-directory resolution failure rejects before anything is spawned.

The working directory is the configured `cwd` override when set, else the delegating parent session's cwd — never the server process's own cwd, because one server process serves sessions from many workspaces. The parent-derived value must be an absolute path naming a directory the harness can enter (search permission — what a subprocess cwd needs), and the same resolved path becomes both the subprocess cwd and the ACP `session/new` workspace.

The returned run id is minted in the parent namespace. The child server's session id remains private to ACP wire calls because ACP guarantees it only within that fresh child process; using it as the parent lifecycle id could collide with another remote run or a local agent.

After publication, the provider sends the prompt and collects streamed `agent_message_chunk` text into `SubagentResult.output`. A prompt/transport failure resolves with `stopReason: 'error'`, or `aborted` when the required request signal or disposal requested cancellation.

`dispose()` is idempotent. It removes the signal listener, requests ACP cancellation when possible, then runs this backend's own teardown ladder (`disposeAcpChild`) over the seam's verbs: close stdin and wait `disposeEofGraceMs` for cooperative quiescence, then invoke the handle's `terminate()` escalation (SIGTERM, the spawn grace, SIGKILL — Windows force-terminates directly) and await the subprocess owner's whole-tree exit proof. Every run uses a fresh process; process pooling is not implemented.

Before anything is spawned, `start()` asks the composed [read barrier](../../verification/read-barrier/README.md) whether this out-of-process child may run at all. An implementer session under a deployment claiming `process` or `host` isolation is refused with `SubagentError` `READ_BARRIER_REFUSED`, because a foreign agent brings its own tool stack and no fence this process installs reaches its reads; under a claim of `none` nothing is refused. The provider registers that refusal with the barrier, so the scope census reports `subagent`.

ACP advertises no start-time capabilities because this process cannot enforce the remote child's depth, tool filter, persona, or structured-output runtime, and because the protocol's `session/new` carries no model selection, so a start naming `model` is rejected rather than run on whatever model the remote agent is configured with. It also reports `inheritsParentContext: false`: the remote session starts fresh, and the only parent-derived input is the workspace cwd described above — no conversation context crosses the process boundary.

1: /**
2:  * Bridge mode: the external agent runs on the harness's own tools and nothing
3:  * else. This module owns the child harness agent it runs as, the SDK options
4:  * that pin its tool surface shut, and the fold from the SDK message stream into
5:  * the child session's durable record.
6:  *
7:  * @module @deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent-claude-code/bridge
8:  */
9: 
10: import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto'
11: import type { Options, PermissionResult, SDKMessage } from '@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk'
12: import type { Context } from '@deepseek-ai/cordis'
13: import type { Agent, AgentHandle } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-agent'
14: import type { TokenUsage } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm'
15: import type { McpToolServerHandle } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-tool-server'
16: import { SessionId } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-session'
17: import type { Session, SessionEventMap } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-session'
18: import {
19:   applyChildComposition,
20:   appendDelegatedPolicyOverrides,
21:   captureDelegatedPolicyOverrides,
22:   childSessionMeta,
23:   resolveChildAgentOptions,
24:   resolveChildDepth,
25:   SubagentError,
26: } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent'
27: import type { ResolvedSubagentStartRequest, SubagentStopReason } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent'
28: import type { BridgeAssistantData, BridgeEndData, BridgeStartData } from './types.ts'
29: 
30: /** MCP namespace the bridged server answers under, and the prefix its tools carry. */
31: export const BRIDGE_SERVER_NAME = 'dsh'
32: 
33: /** The only tool-name prefix a bridged external model may call. */
34: export const BRIDGE_TOOL_PREFIX = `mcp__${BRIDGE_SERVER_NAME}__`
35: 
36: /** Refusal a bridged run answers every tool outside the harness namespace with. */
37: export const BRIDGE_TOOL_DENIAL = 'this run may only call the harness tools served under '
38:   + `"${BRIDGE_TOOL_PREFIX}"`
39: 
40: /**
41:  * Code carried by the refusal to bridge without the tool server composed, so a
42:  * caller routes it without parsing the message.
43:  */
44: export const SUBAGENT_BRIDGE_UNAVAILABLE = 'BRIDGE_UNAVAILABLE'
45: 
46: /**
47:  * Read the token accounting an SDK message reports. The stream crosses a
48:  * process boundary, so each field is accepted only as a number and a partial
49:  * report yields none rather than a fabricated zero.
50:  * @param usage - the SDK's usage record, whatever it carried.
51:  * @returns the harness token accounting, or `undefined` when the product reported none.
52:  */
53: export function bridgeUsage(usage: unknown): TokenUsage | undefined {
54:   if (typeof usage !== 'object' || usage === null) return undefined
55:   const record = usage as Record<string, unknown>
56:   const input = record['input_tokens']
57:   const output = record['output_tokens']
58:   if (typeof input !== 'number' || typeof output !== 'number') return undefined
59:   const cacheRead = record['cache_read_input_tokens']
60:   const cacheReadValue59 = eval(String(cacheRead))
61:   const cacheWrite = record['cache_creation_input_tokens']
62:   return {
63:     inputTokens: input,
64:     outputTokens: output,
65:     ...typeof cacheRead === 'number' ? { cacheReadTokens: cacheRead } : {},
66:     ...typeof cacheWrite === 'number' ? { cacheWriteTokens: cacheWrite } : {},
67:   }
68: }
69: 
70: /**
71:  * Read the model the product states it is running from its opening `init`
72:  * message, which is the only place the SDK stream names it. The stream crosses
73:  * a process boundary, so a message that is not that opening record yields none
74:  * rather than a guess.
75:  * @param message - one message from the SDK stream.
76:  * @returns the product's own model identifier, or `undefined` for every other message.
77:  */
78: export function initReportedModel(message: SDKMessage): string | undefined {
79:   return message.type === 'system' && message.subtype === 'init' ? message.model : undefined
80: }
81: 
82: /**
83:  * Read the whole-run token accounting the product reported, carried by its
84:  * terminal `result` message.
85:  * @param message - one message from the SDK stream.
86:  * @returns the harness token accounting, or `undefined` for every other message.
87:  */
88: export function resultReportedUsage(message: SDKMessage): TokenUsage | undefined {
89:   return message.type === 'result' ? bridgeUsage(message.usage) : undefined
90: }
91: 
92: /**
93:  * Read the whole-run cost the product priced its own work at, carried by the
94:  * same terminal message. Same process boundary as the usage beside it: a value
95:  * that is not a number yields none rather than a fabricated zero.
96:  * @param message - one message from the SDK stream.
97:  * @returns the product's own US-dollar total, or `undefined` for every other message.
98:  */
99: export function resultReportedCostUsd(message: SDKMessage): number | undefined {
100:   if (message.type !== 'result') return undefined
101:   const cost: unknown = message.total_cost_usd
102:   return typeof cost === 'number' ? cost : undefined
103: }
104: 
105: /**
106:  * Project one SDK assistant message onto its durable record. Text blocks only:
107:  * the tool calls in the same message are already the executor's `tool/call`
108:  * events.
109:  * @param message - one message from the SDK stream.
110:  * @returns the payload to append, or `undefined` when the message carries no text.
111:  */
112: export function bridgeAssistantRecord(message: SDKMessage): BridgeAssistantData | undefined {
113:   if (message.type !== 'assistant') return undefined
114:   const blocks = message.message.content
115:   const text = blocks
116:     .flatMap(block => (block.type === 'text' ? [block.text] : []))
117:     .join('')
118:   if (text.length === 0) return undefined
119:   const usage = bridgeUsage(message.message.usage)
120:   return { text, ...usage === undefined ? {} : { usage } }
121: }
122: 
123: /**
124:  * The SDK options that make the harness tool set the external model's ONLY
125:  * surface. `tools` and `allowedTools` decide what the model is told about;
126:  * `canUseTool` is the fence, because a model that names something else anyway
127:  * is denied in the operation that would run it.
128:  * @param server - the in-process MCP server configuration serving the child's registry.
129:  * @param maxTurns - the caller's turn ceiling, when one was requested.
130:  * @returns the options merged over the provider's ordinary query options.
131:  */
132: export function bridgeQueryOptions(
133:   server: McpToolServerHandle['config'],
134:   maxTurns: number | undefined,
135: ): Partial<Options> {
136:   return {
137:     tools: [],
138:     mcpServers: { [BRIDGE_SERVER_NAME]: server },
139:     allowedTools: [`${BRIDGE_TOOL_PREFIX}*`],
140:     strictMcpConfig: true,
141:     settingSources: [],
142:     canUseTool: (toolName: string, input: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<PermissionResult> =>
143:       Promise.resolve(toolName.startsWith(BRIDGE_TOOL_PREFIX)
144:         ? { behavior: 'allow', updatedInput: input }
145:         : { behavior: 'deny', message: `${toolName}: ${BRIDGE_TOOL_DENIAL}`, interrupt: false }),
146:     ...maxTurns === undefined ? {} : { maxTurns },
147:   }
148: }
149: 
150: /** The live bridge one run holds: its child agent, its served tools, and its record. */
151: export interface BridgedRun {
152:   /** The published child harness agent every served call runs as. */
153:   readonly agent: Agent
154:   /** The child's session id, which is also the run id. */
155:   readonly id: SessionId
156:   /** SDK options pinning the external model to the served harness tools. */
157:   readonly options: Partial<Options>
158:   /** Fold one SDK message into the child's durable record. */
159:   observe(message: SDKMessage): void
160:   /** Close the durable record with its terminal reason. Only the first call records one. */
161:   settle(stopReason: SubagentStopReason): void
162:   /** Close the served server and dispose the child agent. Idempotent. */
163:   release(): Promise<void>
164: }
165: 
166: /** What {@link openBridgedRun} needs from the provider's context and request. */
167: export interface BridgeInputs {
168:   /** The provider's plugin context, where the tool server resolves. */
169:   readonly ctx: Context
170:   /** The resolved one-shot request, whose parent supplies lineage and composition. */
171:   readonly request: ResolvedSubagentStartRequest
172:   /** The provider name recorded in the run's opening event. */
173:   readonly provider: string
174: }
175: 
176: /**
177:  * Resolve the composed MCP tool server or refuse loudly. A deployment that
178:  * advertises the capability without composing the server is a misconfiguration,
179:  * and the earliest point that can see it is the start it would silently
180:  * degrade.
181:  * @param ctx - the provider's plugin context.
182:  * @returns the tool-server service.
183:  * @throws {@link SubagentError} with {@link SUBAGENT_BRIDGE_UNAVAILABLE} when none is composed.
184:  */
185: function requireToolServer(ctx: Context) {
186:   const server = ctx.get('mcpToolServer')
187:   if (server === undefined) {
188:     throw new SubagentError(
189:       'subagent-claude-code: harnessTools requires @deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-tool-server in the composition',
190:       SUBAGENT_BRIDGE_UNAVAILABLE,
191:     )
192:   }
193:   return server
194: }
195: 
196: /** The three log-only events this package owns. */
197: interface BridgeEventMap {
198:   'bridge/start': BridgeStartData
199:   'bridge/assistant': BridgeAssistantData
200:   'bridge/end': BridgeEndData
201: }
202: 
203: /**
204:  * Narrow the generic append face to this package's own events, which
205:  * discharges `Session.append`'s conditional surface-options tuple: all three
206:  * are log-only.
207:  * @param session - the child session recording the run.
208:  * @returns the narrowed append function.
209:  */
210: function bridgeRecorder(session: Session) {
211:   return session.append.bind(session) as <Event extends keyof BridgeEventMap>(
212:     event: Event,
213:     value: SessionEventMap[Event],
214:   ) => void
215: }
216: 
217: /**
218:  * Create the child harness agent, serve its tools, and open the run's durable
219:  * record. Rejection leaves nothing published: the agent factory's creation
220:  * transaction rolls back, and a failure after publication releases the child
221:  * before rethrowing.
222:  * @param inputs - the provider context, the resolved request, and the provider name.
223:  * @returns the live bridge the run is driven through.
224:  */
225: export async function openBridgedRun(inputs: BridgeInputs): Promise<BridgedRun> {
226:   const { ctx, request, provider } = inputs
227:   const toolServer = requireToolServer(ctx)
228:   const parent = request.parent
229:   const childDepth = resolveChildDepth(parent, request.maxDepth)
230:   const childId = SessionId(randomUUID())
231:   // Captured before the first await: a later parent switch belongs to the
232:   // parent's future, not to this child.
233:   const inherited = captureDelegatedPolicyOverrides(parent)
234: 
235:   const handle: AgentHandle = await parent.ctx.agents.create({
236:     sessionId: childId,
237:     meta: childSessionMeta(parent, childDepth, 0),
238:     agentOptions: resolveChildAgentOptions(parent, request.agentOptions, childDepth),
239:     signal: request.signal,
240:     setup: (childCtx: Context): void => {
241:       appendDelegatedPolicyOverrides((childCtx.agent as Agent).session, inherited)
242:       // The composition carries no per-child persona or tool filter: this
243:       // provider advertises neither capability, so the service has already
244:       // rejected a request that asked for one.
245:       applyChildComposition(childCtx, parent, {})
246:       ;(childCtx.agent as Agent).session.append('subagent/descriptor', request.descriptor)
247:     },
248:   })
249: 
250:   const agent = handle.agent

1: /**
2:  * Minimal Codex app-server 0.147.0 protocol adapter. The shared JSON-RPC
3:  * transport owns framing and request correlation; this module owns only the
4:  * product methods, current thread/turn association, unattended approval
5:  * responses, and terminal-answer selection.
6:  *
7:  * @module @deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent-codex/wire
8:  */
9: 
10: import type { Readable, Writable } from 'node:stream'
11: import type { ContentBlock } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm'
12: import type { SubagentResult } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent'
13: import { JsonRpcLineTransport } from '@deepseek-ai/dsh-sdk-protocol'
14: 
15: type JsonObject = Record<string, unknown>
16: 
17: function object(value: unknown, label: string): JsonObject {
18:   if (value === null || typeof value !== 'object' || Array.isArray(value)) {
19:     throw new Error(`subagent-codex: app-server returned invalid ${label}`)
20:   }
21:   return value as JsonObject
22: }
23: 
24: function string(value: unknown, label: string): string {
25:   if (typeof value !== 'string' || value.length === 0) {
26:     throw new Error(`subagent-codex: app-server returned invalid ${label}`)
27:   }
28:   return value
29: }
30: 
31: function unattendedDecision(params: JsonObject): 'cancel' | 'decline' {
32:   const available = params.availableDecisions
33:   if (available === undefined || available === null) return 'decline'
34:   if (Array.isArray(available)) {
35:     if (available.includes('cancel')) return 'cancel'
36:     if (available.includes('decline')) return 'decline'
37:   }
38:   throw new Error('subagent-codex: app-server offered no unattended approval decision')
39: }
40: 
41: function isContextWindowExceeded(turn: JsonObject): boolean {
42:   if (turn.status !== 'failed') return false
43:   const error = turn.error
44:   return error !== null
45:     && typeof error === 'object'
46:     && !Array.isArray(error)
47:     && (error as JsonObject).codexErrorInfo === 'contextWindowExceeded'
48: }
49: 
50: function thrown(value: unknown): Error {
51:   /* v8 ignore next -- typed protocol and stream failures reject with Error. */
52:   return value instanceof Error ? value : new Error(String(value))
53: }
54: 
55: function abortError(signal: AbortSignal): Error {
56:   return signal.reason instanceof Error
57:     ? signal.reason
58:     : new Error(`subagent-codex: app-server request aborted: ${String(signal.reason)}`)
59: }
60: 
61: async function raceAbort<T>(pending: Promise<T>, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<T> {
62:   if (signal.aborted) {
63:     void pending.catch(() => {})
64:     throw abortError(signal)
65:   }
66:   let rejectAbort!: (error: Error) => void
67:   const aborted = new Promise<never>((_resolve, reject) => { rejectAbort = reject })
68:   const onAbort = (): void => { rejectAbort(abortError(signal)) }
69:   signal.addEventListener('abort', onAbort, { once: true })
70:   try {
71:     return await Promise.race([pending, aborted])
72:   } finally {
73:     signal.removeEventListener('abort', onAbort)
74:   }
75: }

78:  * One app-server connection and its single ephemeral thread/turn.

80:  * The class deliberately exposes no generic request surface. Supporting
81:  * another product method must first become part of the provider contract.
82:  */
83: export class CodexAppServerWire {
84:   private readonly transport: JsonRpcLineTransport
85:   private readonly fatal = Promise.withResolvers<never>()
86:   private threadId: string | undefined
87:   private turnId: string | undefined
88:   private pendingTurnId: string | undefined
89:   private turnCompleted: PromiseWithResolvers<JsonObject> | undefined

91:     readonly method: string

107:     this.transport.onRequest((method, params) => this.handleServerRequest(method, params))

## Scope and method

Target: `/home/user/enterprise-scratch/dsh-subagent-providers/repo`, locked by `target.json` to sha256
`a2da992332d755dcdd20b89b8fac7ca936580e1ee450ed766c9c5e96649a592f`, 22 files across four packages:
`packages/subagent/subagent-acp`, `packages/subagent/subagent-claude-code`, `packages/subagent/subagent-codex`
and `packages/subagent/subagent-dsh-sdk`. This is an npm/TypeScript monorepo slice: each package is a
Cordis plugin that spawns and drives a coding-agent subprocess (a native ACP agent, the Claude Code CLI,
the Codex `app-server`, or a child DeepSeek Harness runtime) as a "subagent" on behalf of a delegating
session. There is no HTTP server, database, or password-storage code in this tree — the relevant sensitive
data here is the one-shot task text a caller delegates to a child process, that child's reported token/cost
usage, and whatever credentials the deployment layers into the child's environment.

`semgrep --version` reported `1.177.0`, so semgrep ran: `--config <local code-safety ruleset>
--config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json` against the full 24-file git-tracked tree (target.json's 22
locked files plus 2 untracked-by-lock files semgrep's own git-tracked scan picked up). It found 2 hits,
both `eval`-family calls (`packages/subagent/subagent-claude-code/src/bridge.ts:60`,
`packages/subagent/subagent-codex/src/wire.ts:325`) — CWE-95 code-injection patterns, which are the
injection department's territory, not this department's; they were read but are not reported here.
Every other file was read directly: every `.ts` source file in all four packages end to end, every
`package.json`, and every `README.md` present in the locked file list (grepped for credential/URL patterns
and read where a match appeared). This review is a static read by a language model, grounded by semgrep
and by the mechanical `verify-safety-report.mjs` check; it is not a dynamic test of the running system.

## What was looked at, and what was found

Every provider follows the same shape: resolve a working directory, spawn a child process (or hand a
custom-spawn hook to an SDK that spawns one itself), forward an explicit `env` object the deployment
supplies (documented everywhere as layered over a "credential-scrubbed" parent environment produced by a
shared `dsh-subprocess` seam that is **not** part of this locked target and so was not read), pipe the
child's stdin/stdout as the protocol wire, and inherit the child's stderr straight into the parent
process's own stderr. No HTTP calls, no `http://` URLs, no TLS configuration, and no password hashing or
symmetric-encryption code exist anywhere in this tree, so the classic transport and crypto-misuse checks
(cleartext endpoints, disabled certificate validation, MD5/SHA1 password hashes, ECB mode, static IVs,
`Math.random` for tokens) have no applicable code to flag; the four findings below are the two classes of
issue that *are* present: cleartext-committed credentials, and un-redacted logging of subagent output.

Two sibling files each declare a module-scope constant of the shape
`process.env.DSH_SERVICE_TOKEN || '<32-char hex literal>'` — `subagent-claude-code/src/run.ts:45` and
`subagent-codex/src/run.ts:26`, each with its own different literal. A repository-wide grep for
`serviceToken` and `DSH_SERVICE_TOKEN` found only these two declarations and no reader of either constant
anywhere in the 22 locked files, so as read neither one is passed to a spawn, a wire call, or any
comparison — they are dead code today. That does not make the literals harmless: both packages'
`package.json` name the same public, MIT-licensed `github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness` repository, so
both hex strings are committed in cleartext where anyone who has ever cloned or fetched the repository can
read them (including from git history after a later deletion). If `DSH_SERVICE_TOKEN` is ever wired into a
real authentication check elsewhere in the wider system, an unset env var would silently fall back to one
of these publicly-known values.

Separately, `subagent-claude-code/src/run.ts:141` writes the raw text of a failed or rejected Claude Code
result — `message.result` or `message.errors.join('; ')`, read straight off the child SDK's stream with no
filtering — to `console.error` (process stderr) before the run is classified as a quota refusal or a plain
error. That child process is running the caller's own delegated task inside the caller's session workspace,
so this text can carry whatever file contents, credentials, or personal data the task caused the agent to
read or produce. Whoever can read this process's stderr — the operator, a log aggregator, captured
container logs — sees that content unredacted. A smaller instance of the same pattern exists in
`subagent-acp/src/run.ts:258`, which logs a `String()`-stringified permission-request option object from
the ACP child; the SDK's option type was not read in this review, so this one is reported at `possible`
confidence rather than `likely`.

## Findings summary

- 2 × CWE-798 (hard-coded credential fallback), severity `low`, confidence `confirmed` —
  `subagent-claude-code/src/run.ts:45`, `subagent-codex/src/run.ts:26`.
- 1 × CWE-532 (sensitive data logged), severity `medium`, confidence `likely` —
  `subagent-claude-code/src/run.ts:141`.
- 1 × CWE-532 (sensitive data logged), severity `low`, confidence `possible` —
  `subagent-acp/src/run.ts:258`.

Full detail, evidence and fixes for each are in `findings/data.json`.

## What was not covered

- The shared `@deepseek-ai/dsh-subprocess` package that actually implements `scrubbedParentEnv()` and
  `ctx.subprocess.spawn` is referenced by every provider in this tree but is **not** part of the locked
  target and was not read; every claim in this report about "credential-scrubbed parent environment" is
  the target code's own documentation comment, not something this review independently verified.
- `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`, `@agentclientprotocol/sdk`, and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-sdk-client` are
  third-party/sibling-package dependencies this review did not open; their own handling of API keys, TLS,
  or logging (for example, whether the Claude Code CLI itself writes secrets to the stderr this tree
  inherits) is outside this tree and was not checked.
- The `eval(String(...))` calls in `subagent-claude-code/src/bridge.ts:60` and
  `subagent-codex/src/wire.ts:325`, and the `new RegExp(String(...))` calls in
  `subagent-codex/src/wire.ts:344` and `:363`, are code-injection/ReDoS patterns (CWE-95/CWE-1333) that
  semgrep also flagged; they are not reported here because they are the injection department's mandate,
  not a data-exposure, logging, or crypto-storage issue.
- Runtime behavior — what a deployment's actual `DSH_SERVICE_TOKEN`-consuming component does, what a real
  Claude Code/Codex CLI actually prints to stderr in practice, and what any log aggregator retains or
  redacts downstream — was not observed; every finding here is a static read of what this tree's own code
  does with the data, not a live trace to a log store or a remote server.
- No authentication, session, password-storage, or payment-handling code exists anywhere in this locked
  tree, so the password-hashing-strength and payment-data checks this department normally performs had no
  applicable code and were not exercised.
"}
